x: University residences, private rooms, contracts and how to avoid scams.

For the visa you must show suitable accommodation in Italy. An application for a student residence alone is not enough. Student residences are run by the regional DSU agencies and some universities. Places are limited, and you apply through the yearly call. A rental contract must be registered with the Agenzia delle Entrate within 30 days of signing. Whoever hosts you or rents you a room must tell the police within 48 hours (dichiarazione di ospitalità). Never pay before you have seen the room (in person or by video call) and the contract.

Your region's DSU agency: student residences, often linked to the DSU scholarship. See the scholarships guide. Your university's housing office: many have lists of rooms or partner residences. Private rooms: websites, student groups and agencies. Prices depend a lot on the city and the area. For your first weeks, a hotel or short stay gives you time to visit rooms in person.

Ask for a written contract and check how long it lasts, the deposit, and what the rent includes (bills, internet). The contract must be registered within 30 days. Ask the landlord for proof of registration: you may need it for your residence permit. The owner must send the hospitality declaration to the police within 48 hours. Keep a copy.

Do not send money by transfer or money service to someone you have not met, for a room you have not seen. Be careful with prices much lower than others in the same area, and with owners who are "abroad" and cannot show the room. Check that the person is the owner or a real agency, and pay the deposit only with a signed contract. If in doubt, ask your university's housing office.

Which entrance test you need for each type of program in Italy: IMAT, the filter semester, TOLC, CEnT-S, private university tests and Bocconi. There is no single entrance exam for Italian universities. The test you need depends on three things: the program, the language it is taught in, and whether the university is public or private. This page explains the most common tests. The call for applications (bando) of your program always has the final word, so read it first.

Programs with national limited places (medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, health professions, architecture): the Ministry sets the number of places and the test is the same everywhere. Programs with local limited places: each university chooses its own test, very often a TOLC. Open-access programs: there is no competition for places, but many ask for a test to check your level. If your score is low, you get extra learning requirements (OFA) to complete in your first year. Master's degrees (laurea magistrale): usually no entrance exam. The university assesses your file. Private universities: their own tests and calendars, often months earlier than public universities.

h: 2. Medicine in English at public universities: IMAT
x: IMAT (International Medical Admissions Test) is the national test for Medicine and Surgery, Dentistry and Veterinary Medicine taught in English at public universities. Italian, EU and non-EU candidates can take it, in Italy or at some authorised centres abroad. The filter semester does not apply to these programs: if you pass, you enrol directly in October. Section Questions Biology 23 Chemistry 15 Physics and mathematics 13 Logical reasoning and problems 5 Reading skills and knowledge from studies 4 Format: 60 multiple-choice questions with 5 options, in 100 minutes, all in English. No calculator. Scoring: +1.5 for a correct answer, −0.4 for a wrong one, 0 if blank. Maximum 90 points. Minimum score: EU candidates and those treated as EU need at least 20 points to enter the ranking. Non-EU candidates living abroad only need a score above zero. The real cut-off is higher: in 2025 the first allocation for medicine closed at 54.8 points, and the most requested universities were above 60. Places: in 2026, 1,207 places in medicine in English for EU candidates (up from 952), plus dentistry, 45 places in veterinary medicine and separate places for non-EU candidates living abroad. Registration: on Universitaly only, within the dates of the yearly decree. You list your universities in order of preference, and you cannot change them after registration closes. 2026 dates: registration 26 August – 9 September, test on 29 September, national ranking on 26 October. 2027: the decree is expected in July or August 2027 and the test at the end of September 2027. These are estimates, not official dates. English certificate: not needed to sit the test, but some universities ask for one when you enrol.

h: 3. Medicine in Italian at public universities: the filter semester
x: Since 2025/2026 there is no entrance test for medicine, dentistry and veterinary medicine taught in Italian at public universities. Instead, anyone with a secondary school diploma enrols in an open first semester (semestre filtro), studies three subjects and takes three national exams. A national ranking then decides who continues. Places are still limited: 18,889 places in medicine for 2026/2027. Who can enrol: Italian, EU and non-EU students with a secondary school diploma, with no age limit and a maximum of three attempts. Registration: on Universitaly (in 2026: 13 July – 3 August), fee €250. You choose at least 10 universities for medicine and at least 5 for a related back-up program. Attendance is compulsory. If you do not meet it, you cannot take the exams. Exams: Biology, Chemistry and introductory biochemistry, and Physics. Each exam has 31 questions (21 multiple-choice and 10 fill-in) in 50 minutes, on paper, without a periodic table. +1 for a correct answer, −0.10 for a wrong one. You need at least 18/30 in each subject. Ranking in three groups: three exams passed (+300), two (+200), one (+100). A student who passes all three always ranks ahead of one who passes two. 2026/2027 dates: exams on 10 December 2026 and 11 January 2027 (the better grade counts), ranking on 22 January 2027. Registration for 2027/2028 usually opens in July. If you are not admitted: you can move to the related program you chose (for example biotechnology, biological sciences, pharmacy or nursing) with your credits recognised, enrol in another program until 12 March 2027, or try again next year. Non-EU candidates living abroad have a separate ranking. Free official practice: semestreaperto-medodovet.it.

h: 4. Most bachelor’s programs taught in Italian: TOLC
x: TOLC (Test OnLine CISIA) is the most common test for bachelor's programs at public universities. CISIA is a consortium of more than 60 universities. The university decides which TOLC you need, and the same subject can use different TOLCs at different universities. TOLC Programs Questions and time (without English) TOLC-I Engineering and technical programs 50 in 110 min TOLC-E Economics, statistics, social sciences 36 in 90 min TOLC-F Pharmacy, some science and sport science programs 50 in 72 min TOLC-B Biology, biotechnology 50 in 110 min TOLC-S Science (STEM) 55 in 120 min TOLC-PSI Psychology 50 in 100 min TOLC-SU Humanities 50 in 100 min TOLC-SPS Political and social sciences 40 in 90 min TOLC-AV Agriculture and veterinary-related bachelor's programs 50 in 100 min TOLC-LP Professional-oriented degrees 30 in 90 min Every TOLC ends with an English section: 30 questions in 15 minutes. Scoring: +1 for a correct answer, −0.25 for a wrong one, 0 if blank (no penalty in the English section). No calculator. Cost: €35 in 2026, not refundable. Retakes: the same TOLC once per calendar month. The university decides whether your best or your latest score counts. Where: at a university (TOLC@UNI) or from home with online supervision (TOLC@CASA). Not every program accepts TOLC@CASA. Validity: your result counts for every program that uses the same TOLC, at least for the calendar year you took it. Taking the test does not enrol you. You must still apply to the university. Book on testcisia.it. The 2027 dates were not published yet on 29 October 2026.

Since November 2025, CISIA has replaced the English TOLCs with one test, CEnT-S, for English-taught programs in engineering, economics, pharmacy and other sciences. 65 questions in 6 sections, 140 minutes. Cost €55. One attempt per period. From 2026/2027 there are five periods, from November to September. Tests run in the afternoon only. Scores are normalised at the end of each period. You can take it at a university (CEnT@UNI) or from home (CEnT@casa).

Private universities do not use IMAT or the filter semester. Each one has its own test and ranking, usually between February and April. You can apply to several in the same year. Figures below are from the 2026/2027 calls, as a guide until the new calls come out. University Language Test Test fee Yearly fees Campus Bio-Medico (Rome) Italian and English 60 questions (biology, chemistry, physics) in 100 min, in person, one session €170 €15,640 Italian / €19,140 English Humanitas (Milan) English only HUMAT: 60 questions in 120 min, from home, two rounds €200 €10,156–23,156, based on income Cattolica (Rome) Italian and English 65 questions in 65 min (logic, sciences, maths, ethics and religious culture) €250 €6,900–18,598 in the first year, based on income San Raffaele (Milan) Italian and English 60 questions in 60 min (sciences only), from home, two sessions €200–300 €20,190–20,690 UniCamillus (Rome, Venice, Cefalù) Italian and English 60 questions in 60 min (logic, sciences, humanitarian topics), from home €180 €16,500 Italian / €21,000 English Expected for 2027/2028: Campus Bio-Medico call at the end of October 2026 with the test in mid-February; Humanitas call between October and November; Cattolica and San Raffaele calls at the end of January. The first instalment after admission is usually not refundable (between €2,500 and €7,500). Compare all your dates before you pay. Other private universities with medicine: LUM (Bari), Link Campus, Università Europea di Roma, Kore (Enna).

Accepted tests for bachelor's programs: the Bocconi online test, the SAT or the ACT. For law programs only, also the LSAT or the Bocconi online test – Law. Selection: your test score counts for 55% and your grades in the last years of secondary school for 45%. Attempts: up to 4 attempts at the Bocconi test for 2027/2028. 2027/2028 dates for international applicants: book the online test by 19 January 2027; the winter application round runs from 25 November 2026 to 26 January 2027. Up to 50–55% of places in English-taught programs may be reserved for international applicants.

Most master's programs at public universities have no national test. The university checks your file and whether you meet the course requirements. Usual documents: bachelor's diploma and transcript, CV, motivation letter, language certificate, sometimes recommendation letters. Pre-assessment: many universities have their own portal for applicants with foreign qualifications, with deadlines that are often months earlier than for Italian students. Interviews: some programs add an online interview. GMAT or GRE: mainly asked by competitive economics and management programs. Check the program page.

All of these are free. Some need a free account. IMAT: past papers are public. This guide lists where to find them and other simulators: TestBuddy: where to practise for IMAT (a private preparation site, not an official page). TOLC: simulations with the real structure and timing, and past tests with explained solutions, in the CISIA practice area (free registration). CEnT-S: CISIA added simulations of the new test to the same practice area (CISIA announcement, CEnT-S page). Filter semester: the official free platform by CRUI and MUR, with basic exercises and simulations in the exam format: semestreaperto-medodovet.it. Private universities and Bocconi: each university publishes its own sample questions or practice tests on its admissions page. Check the page of the university you want.

h: Summary: which test for which program?
x: Program Test Usual period Fee Medicine in English, public IMAT end of September set by the yearly decree Medicine in Italian, public Filter semester registration in July, exams December–January €250 Medicine, private Each university's test (HUMAT and others) February–April €170–300 Engineering, economics, sciences, pharmacy, psychology, humanities (in Italian) TOLC (type depends on the program) January–November €35 Engineering, economics, pharmacy, sciences (in English) CEnT-S five periods, November–September €55 Bocconi bachelor's Bocconi online test, SAT or ACT September–January set by Bocconi Master's degrees File assessment, sometimes GMAT/GRE often December–May set by the university For language certificates, read language requirements. For documents, Universitaly pre-enrolment and the visa, read how to apply.

Tuition fees, taxes, the money you must show for your visa, and scholarships that help. Every university in Italy sets its own fees. Use this page to understand how costs work, then check the exact amounts on your university's fees page ("tasse e contributi").

h: 1. Money you must show for your visa
x: To get a study visa, you must prove that you have enough money to live in Italy. For the academic year 2026/2027 the Ministry of University and Research (MUR) sets this at €10,179.85 per year. The money must come from legal sources that can be traced. It should preferably be your own money or your family's. You also need health insurance that covers medical care and hospital stays. See the health insurance guide. This is not a fee you pay. It is money you must show you have.

At public universities you do not pay one fixed price. Fees are made of three parts: Part What it is Example amount (2026/2027) Regional tax for the right to study Paid every year, goes to the region's student services €140 at the University of Tuscia (Lazio) Stamp duty (imposta di bollo) A fixed state charge €16 University contribution The main fee, set by each university Depends on your family's income and assets The no-tax area. By national rules, students whose family ISEE is up to €22,000 pay no university contribution if they meet the other conditions (Ministerial Decree 1014 of 3 August 2021). Many universities go higher: for example, the University of Tuscia's no-tax area reaches €26,000 for 2026/2027.

h: 3. If your family’s income is abroad
x: If your family's income and assets are abroad, you cannot use a normal Italian ISEE. Universities handle this in different ways: A special ISEE for income abroad (ISEE parificato, also called ISEUP at some universities), prepared by an authorised tax office (CAF) in Italy. A fixed fee based on your country. For example, at the University of Tuscia students without this ISEE pay a fixed amount from €600 to €1,950 a year, depending on their country's income level. At the University of Turin, fees for students with income abroad go from €500 to €1,500 a year, based on their country's income per person, plus €156 for the regional tax and stamp duty. Particularly poor countries. The Ministry publishes a list of countries whose students get special treatment (for 2026/2027: Ministerial Decree 176 of 24 February 2026). At the University of Turin, students from these countries pay only the first instalment of €156. Rules change from year to year and from one university to another. Always read your university's fees page for the current year. To compare universities, see our tuition fees by university page.

Non-state universities (for example LUISS, Bocconi or Cattolica) and online universities set their own fees. Check the fees page on each university's website. You can find every university's website in our university guide.

Every region funds right-to-study (DSU) scholarships, and international students can apply. Each region sets its own income limits and amounts, so check your region's call. For example, the University of Verona's 2026/2027 call (Veneto region) uses: Family ISEE up to €26,306.25 and ISPE up to €43,125.94. For students living away from home (fuori sede): €8,246 a year for the lowest incomes, €7,171.11 in the middle band, and gradually less (down to €3,585.50) near the income limit. At Verona, part of it is kept back to pay for meals and, if you get one, a room in a student residence. Students from particularly poor countries need a certificate from the Italian embassy in their country instead of an ISEE parificato. Calls often close before classes start, so check the deadline early (Verona's 2026/2027 call closed on 30 September 2026). Read the scholarships and funding guide for more.
Rent, food and transport depend a lot on the city. The regional DSU agency and your university's housing office are the best places to find rooms in student residences. See the accommodation guide.
A short checklist for the days after you arrive: residence permit, codice fiscale, health, phone, bank and enrolment.

Within 8 working days: apply for your residence permit at the post office. Codice fiscale: your Italian tax code. You need it for almost everything. Health: make sure your insurance is valid, or register with the national health service. University: finish your enrolment so your visa is not revoked.

Residence permit. Get the yellow kit at the post office and send it within 8 working days of arriving. Keep the receipt with your passport. See the residence permit guide. Codice fiscale. If you are a non-EU student staying more than 90 days, the Questura assigns it during your residence permit process. You can also ask for it at an Italian consulate before you leave, or at an Agenzia delle Entrate office in Italy. Many universities help with this too. Health cover. Keep your private insurance valid, or register with the national health service (SSN) at your local health office. See the health insurance guide. Enrolment. Finish your enrolment at the university and pay the fees. If you are not enrolled on Universitaly by 31 January, your visa will be revoked. Phone. Phone shops usually ask for your passport and your codice fiscale to sell you a SIM card. An Italian number is useful for the Questura and the university. Bank account. Banks and online banks usually ask for your passport, codice fiscale and an address in Italy. Compare monthly fees before you choose. Transport. Many cities and regions have cheaper passes for students. Ask your university or the local transport company. Accommodation. If someone hosts you or rents you a room, they must tell the police within 48 hours. See the accommodation guide. Your university's international office is the best place to ask when something is not clear.
Regional DSU scholarships, Italian government scholarships, university waivers and other funding.

The biggest help for most students is the regional DSU scholarship: money, and sometimes a room and meals. It depends on your family income, with limits that differ from region to region. International students usually need an ISEE parificato, or a certificate from the Italian embassy if they come from a particularly poor country. The Italian government (MAECI) also offers scholarships through the Study in Italy portal. The 2026/2027 call closed in March 2026. Calls close early, often before classes start. Check the dates as soon as you choose your university.

Each region funds scholarships for students enrolled in its universities, including international students. Depending on the region, the call is run by a regional DSU agency or by the university itself, and each region sets its own income limits and amounts. For example, the University of Verona's 2026/2027 call (Veneto region) uses: Family ISEE up to €26,306.25 and ISPE up to €43,125.94. For students who live away from their family: €8,246 per year for the lowest incomes, €7,171.11 in the middle band, and gradually less (down to €3,585.50) near the income limit. You also need to pass a minimum number of credits each year to keep the scholarship. Read your region's call carefully.

If your family's income and property are abroad, you need an ISEE parificato, issued in Italy by an authorised tax assistance centre (CAF) using documents from your country. Students from the ministry's list of particularly poor countries need a certificate from the Italian embassy instead. Start early: documents from your country may need translation and legalisation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs offers scholarships to foreign students from the countries on its list. You apply only through Study in Italy. The 2026/2027 call closed on 26 March 2026, so check the portal early for the next one.
Many universities have their own scholarships or lower fees for international students. Look at the "scholarships" or "fees" page of each university.
Some governments, foundations and international organisations fund study abroad. Ask in your country too. See the full list in our scholarships directory, and how fees work in How much it costs.
Private insurance or the national health service (SSN): what students need and how to register.

You need health insurance for the visa and for the residence permit. After you arrive, you have two options: private insurance or registering with the national health service (SSN). SSN registration for non-EU students costs €700 per calendar year (January to December), as several universities state. With the SSN you choose a family doctor (medico di base), whose visits are free. In an emergency, call 112 (118 also works for an ambulance).

You can keep an insurance policy that is valid in Italy for your whole stay. Check before you buy that it covers hospital care with no limits for urgent treatment, because the Questura checks this. Some universities suggest specific policies; ask your international office.

Pay the €700 fee for the year (the payment method depends on the region: some use an F24 form, others a postal slip). Go to the local health office of your area (called ASL, ASP or ATS depending on the region). Bring: the payment receipt, your passport, your codice fiscale, your residence permit or its receipt, and proof of enrolment or of your address. Choose your family doctor. If you have a regular employment contract in Italy, you can register with the SSN for free instead of paying the €700. Ask your local health office. Registration ends on 31 December, whenever you pay, so registering late in the year covers only a few months. For this reason, Università Cattolica advises students who arrive in September to buy 12 months of private insurance first, and then register with the SSN.
EU students can use their European health insurance card (TEAM) for necessary care. For full SSN registration, ask your home health service for form S1 before you leave.

Call 112 for emergencies (118 also works for an ambulance). At night and on holidays, the guardia medica (out-of-hours doctor) can help. For serious problems, go to the pronto soccorso (emergency department) of a hospital.

The steps from choosing a program to enrolling, for students living outside the EU. This guide is for students who are not EU citizens and live outside Italy. It follows the official rules of the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR) for the academic years 2026/2027 and 2027/2028. Each university can add its own rules and earlier deadlines, so always read the page of the program you want.

h: 1. Choose a program and check the requirements
x: Use our university guide to find universities, then open each university's official list of programs. For a bachelor's or single-cycle degree you need: A secondary school certificate after at least 12 years of schooling. If your country has a university entrance exam, the certificate showing you passed it. For a master's degree you need: An official first-cycle degree (bachelor's level) that, in your country, lets you continue to a master's. A transcript of your exams and course contents. Language: For programs taught in Italian, you need Italian at B2 level at least. Each university runs its own test, preferably online, before you apply for the visa. Some certificates exempt you, for example the Perugia or Siena diploma of Italian language and culture, or CLIQ certificates at C1 or C2. For programs taught in another language, such as English, you need a certificate in that language at B2 level at least, covering all four skills. Programs with an entrance exam: Architecture and Primary Education have an entrance exam. Medicine, Dentistry and Veterinary Medicine follow special national rules (Law 26/2025). Check the program page for dates.

Your original diploma (or degree) and, for master's applicants, your transcript. A document that shows the value and authenticity of your qualification: a CIMEA statement (comparability and verification) or a Declaration of Value (Dichiarazione di valore) from the Italian embassy. If your country follows the Lisbon Convention, you may be able to download the comparability statement from CIMEA's ARDI service. A Diploma Supplement, if your university issues one. Translations into Italian, where needed (for programs taught in English, the transcript may not need translating). Your language certificate. If your final certificate is not ready yet, a provisional certificate from the official authority in your country is accepted. Self-declarations are not.

Many universities ask you to apply first through their own admission portal, with their own deadlines. For example, Ca' Foscari University of Venice accepts applications only through its online portal, not by email. The university checks your documents and decides whether to admit you.

Universitaly is the free, official portal for pre-enrolment. You fill in your pre-application there, and the university validates it online. Only students with a validated pre-application can apply for a study visa. Being admitted by the university does not guarantee a visa, and a visa does not guarantee enrolment.

With your validated pre-application, apply at the Italian embassy or consulate in your country of residence for a type D study visa ("Immatricolazione Università"). Deadline for the academic year 2026/2027: 30 November 2026. For 2027/2028: 31 October 2027. Universities can set earlier deadlines. You must show €10,179.85 per year of legal, traceable funds, suitable accommodation in Italy and health insurance. See How much it costs. Read the study visa guide for the full checklist.

Within 8 working days of arriving, apply for your residence permit for study. See the residence permit guide. Complete your enrolment at the university. University fees are usually paid before enrolment is finished, which happens after you receive your visa. Students who are not enrolled on Universitaly by 31 January of the academic year will have their visa revoked, and the Questura is informed.

Which English or Italian level you usually need, which certificates count, and when you can be exempt. This page gives the general rules that apply at most Italian universities. Each university, and often each programme, sets its own exact level, accepted certificates and scores. Always check the page of the programme you want before you apply.

Usual level: B2. Most universities ask for at least B2 English. A few programmes accept B1, and some competitive master's programmes ask for C1. Common certificates: IELTS Academic, TOEFL iBT, Cambridge English (B2 First, C1 Advanced) and PTE Academic. As a rough guide, requirements range from about IELTS 5.0 to 6.5, or TOEFL iBT about 59 to 94, and are usually higher for master's programmes. Duolingo English Test: accepted by only some universities. Others say clearly that they do not accept it. Common exemptions: being a native speaker or a citizen of an English-speaking country, or having completed a previous degree taught entirely in English. Some universities accept a letter from your university saying your studies were in English; others do not. Without a certificate: some universities check your English with their own test or during an interview.

Level: B2. National rules require at least B2 Italian for students who live outside the EU and need a visa. The university's own test: each university checks your Italian with its own test, usually online and before the visa application. Several universities use the same shared online test (for example the CISIA TEST ITA L2). Certificates: recognised Italian certificates (CILS, CELI, CERT.IT and PLIDA, which belong to the CLIQ group) at B2 or higher are accepted by many universities. A C1 or C2 CLIQ certificate, or the diploma of the Universities for Foreigners of Perugia or Siena, exempts you from the test.

h: 3. If you study in English, do you need Italian?
x: Usually not at entry. Some universities still ask you to reach a basic level of Italian during your studies or before you graduate. Learning some Italian also makes daily life much easier.

Some universities want the certificate when you apply, others accept it later, before enrolment. Some only accept recent certificates, for example from the last three years. Check the dates on the programme page, and see How to apply for the full steps. You can find each university's website in our universities guide.

How Palestinians apply to study in Italy, the scholarships for Palestinian students and researchers, the situation of students from Gaza, and the organisations that help. Important. Most of the calls on this page are closed, but many universities repeat them every year, usually between April and September. Use the dates below to know when to look, and always read the current call on the university's site. Corso Italy is not linked to any of these programmes or organisations.

h: 1. The normal way to study in Italy
x: Palestinian students apply like any other student from outside the European Union. See our guides on how to apply and the study visa. What is specific to Palestinians: Where to apply for the visa: if you live in the Palestinian territories, at the Consulate General of Italy in Jerusalem, by booking on Prenot@mi. If you cannot reach the Consulate, you can apply at the VFS Global centre in Ramallah, by appointment. If you live in another country (Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt…), you apply at the Italian embassy or consulate there. Pre-enrolment: online on Universitaly. The university must validate it before you apply for the visa. Your diploma: the Tawjihi or your degree, with a CIMEA attestation or a Dichiarazione di valore, and a certified Italian translation. Language: B2 in Italian for Italian-taught programmes, or B2 in English for English-taught programmes. Money: you must show €10,179.85 a year, plus about €500 for the return flight. Bank statements must cover the last six months. A scholarship or a guarantor in Italy also counts. Cash and property do not. Deadline: apply for the visa by 30 November 2026 for 2026/27, and by 31 October 2027 for 2027/28. Fees: Palestine is not on the 2026 list of particularly poor countries (Ministerial Decree 176/2026). So you usually need an ISEE parificato (see costs), or you pay the fixed fee the university sets for your country. Italian Government scholarships (MAECI): students from Palestine can apply on the Study in Italy portal. The 2026/27 call closed on 26 March 2026.

IUPALS (Italian Universities for Palestinian Students) was run by the Conference of Italian University Rectors (CRUI) with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of University and Research, for 2025/26. It offered 97 scholarships at 35 universities, for bachelor's and master's degrees, to students living in the Palestinian territories. Each scholarship covered at least tuition, accommodation, meals, health insurance and the flight to Italy, plus an Italian course in Bethlehem and Ramallah. For 2026/27: the University of Padova states that no new edition is planned. The National Council of University Students (CNSU) has asked the ministries to fund it again.

These calls closed in 2025 and 2026. Most are for students who live in the Palestinian territories and are not yet enrolled at an Italian university. Students from Gaza can only leave through evacuations organised by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for students who already have an admission or a scholarship from an Italian university. There is no form to apply for evacuation yourself: the university and the Consulate in Jerusalem coordinate the list. The route: the Kerem Shalom crossing, then the Allenby crossing into Jordan, a night at the Italian Hospital in Amman, then a flight to Rome. Numbers: 157 students in four operations between September and December 2025, 72 on 11 May 2026, 17 on 2 June 2026 and 25 in September 2026. In total, 271 students since September 2025. Pause: evacuations stopped between December 2025 and spring 2026. In February 2026 the Consulate had 165 requests. The obstacles reported by universities, lawyers and the press: Each departure needs the approval of Israel and Jordan. Italian language: in June 2026 some students were blocked because a B2 certificate in Italian was asked for. A circular of 3 July 2026 told universities that the certificate is secondary for students from war zones. Money for the visa: being admitted does not give you the right to a visa. The scholarship must reach €10,179.85 a year, or a guarantor must cover the rest. In Genoa, for example, 84 students were admitted but only 18 could be funded. Family: evacuation does not include family members. After you get your residence permit, you can ask for family reunification at the Prefettura of the city where you live. Online tests: online admission tests are very hard to take from Gaza. For open-access programmes, a certificate of attendance was accepted instead.

Official offices Consulate General of Italy in Jerusalem: visas, and the list of students from Gaza who have an admission or a scholarship. Italian Embassy in Amman and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: they organise the evacuations. The international office of your university: most universities have a contact for Palestinian students (for example iupals@polito.it at the Politecnico di Torino). Legal help ASGI (Association for Legal Studies on Immigration): its lawyers follow the cases of students from Gaza and requests for humanitarian visas, including appeals in the courts in Rome. Housing and reception Diocese of Rome and the Community of Sant'Egidio: with Sapienza, free housing for students from Gaza until March 2029, and Italian classes. Caritas: accommodation for some students. ARCI, ACLI and Coop: among the groups that help fund the University of Milan's scholarships. Solidarity associations Assopace Palestina: supports students from Gaza in Italy. In August 2026 it hosted 50 of them for a week. Fiori dai cannoni: a campaign by the publisher Another Coffee Stories, asking for "educational corridors" and emergency visas for students from Gaza who have been admitted to Italian universities. PASS (Palestinian students support): an informal group of volunteers who help Palestinian students with paperwork, especially at art and music academies (AFAM). Students National Council of University Students (CNSU): it asks for a new national scholarship programme, one website for all scholarships, and more flexibility on documents and language.

Watch for calls from April to September, and apply to several universities. Complete your Universitaly pre-enrolment and ask for the CIMEA attestation early. Check that your scholarship, or a guarantor, covers €10,179.85 a year, or the visa can be refused. If you are in Gaza and receive an admission or a scholarship, tell the university at once so that it can add you to the Consulate's list.

Who can apply for a PhD (dottorato di ricerca) in Italy, how much the scholarship is, when the calls open, how the selection works, and the visa and permit after admission. In short. A PhD in Italy (dottorato di ricerca) lasts at least three years, full time. Most places come with a scholarship of at least €16,243 gross a year, and there are no tuition fees. Each university publishes its own call (bando) once or several times a year, usually between January and September. To see when each university's call closed last year, how much it paid and whether the interview could be online, see PhD calls by university. We use the 2026/27 call of the University of Tuscia as the main example. Other universities follow the same national rules, but details (dates, documents, fees) change: always read the call of the university you choose.

Duration: at least 3 years, full time. Some programmes last 4 years. Cycles: each year's intake is called a ciclo. The 42nd cycle started on 1 November 2026, the 43rd will start in autumn 2027. A few programmes start on another date (for example 11 September 2026 for the first call at Politecnico di Milano, 1 December 2026 at Humanitas). Language: many programmes are taught and examined in English. The call says which languages you can use for the project and the interview.

Degree: an Italian laurea magistrale (or an older equivalent), or a foreign degree of the same level. There is no age limit and no citizenship requirement. If you have not graduated yet: you can usually apply, but you must get your degree by the date in the call (31 October 2026 at Tuscia). If you don't, you lose the place. Foreign degree: the selection committee decides whether it is equivalent, for this call only. Tuscia asks for the master's degree certificate with the grade, the certificate of a degree that lasted at least four years with the grade, and the transcript of records with the grading scale. Documents in languages other than Italian, English or French need an official translation. A second scholarship is not possible: if you already had a PhD scholarship, you can only apply for a place without a scholarship. A foreign language: you need to know at least one, and it is tested at the interview.

With a scholarship (con borsa): most places. Without a scholarship (senza borsa): you study without being paid, but you don't pay tuition fees. Reserved places: for employees of companies or public bodies, and sometimes for holders of foreign degrees or of a scholarship from their own government. Some scholarships are tied to a set topic (tematica vincolata): your research must be on that topic.

Minimum: €16,243 gross a year (ministerial decree 247/2022), paid monthly. Social security contributions (INPS) are deducted, so the net amount is lower. The scholarship is exempt from income tax. Some universities pay more. In the 42nd cycle, for example: Brescia €18,432.84, Politecnico di Torino €18,854.52, Humanitas €21,000, the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano €28,000. Abroad: the scholarship goes up by 50% during authorised research periods abroad, for up to 12 months (18 months with joint supervision, co-tutela). Research budget: at least 10% of the scholarship each year, also for students without a scholarship. Fees: no tuition fees. At Tuscia you pay only the regional tax (€140) and the stamp duty (€16) each year, plus €25 to apply.

There is no national date. Last year's calls closed from January (SISSA, Luiss) to September, and some universities have two or three rounds: the Politecnico di Torino's second round closes on 16 November 2026 and its third on 15 February 2027. Our list by university shows the dates for each university we checked, and which calls are still open. To find calls: the PhD page of each university (look for Dottorato di ricerca or Bando); the Ministry of University and Research database, which lists PhD calls from Italian universities. Start preparing early: a good research project takes months.

h: 6. How to apply, step by step
x: Choose a programme and read its call and annex (allegato or scheda). The annex has what matters: number of scholarships, topics, documents and how the selection works. Prepare the documents. Usually: a CV; a research project, which is the most important document (the call says how long it can be); a motivation letter; your degree certificates and transcripts; sometimes reference letters (Cagliari, for example, asks for them) or your master's thesis. Apply online only, on the university's portal (often PICA or Esse3). At Tuscia each file must be a PDF of at most 10 MB. Pay the application fee with pagoPA. At Tuscia, a missing payment means exclusion. Ask for an online interview when you apply, if you live abroad. At several universities (Padova, Florence, Tuscia) you can only ask in the application.

The committee assesses your qualifications and project. Some programmes add a written test, and almost all have an oral interview about your project. Results are published as a ranking for each type of place. At Tuscia, if two candidates have the same score, the younger one goes first. If someone who was admitted withdraws, the next person on the list takes the place (scorrimento). Keep checking the rankings after they are published.

Enrol quickly: at Tuscia within 3 days of the email. Visa: if you need one, it is a study visa (type D), with pre-enrolment on Universitaly. The university gives you an admission letter for the embassy. See our visa guide. Starting from home: at Tuscia, students waiting for their visa can start remotely and must arrive in Italy by 30 November 2026. Residence permit: apply within 8 working days of arriving, with the kit from the post office. It is renewed every year. See our residence permit guide.

Full time: any paid work needs the approval of the board of professors (Collegio dei docenti) and must respect the rules in force. Extension: you can ask once, in the last year, for up to 12 more months to finish the thesis, for documented reasons and without a scholarship. Extensions and suspensions together cannot be longer than 18 months, except for maternity or paternity leave and other cases set by law. The end: you write a thesis, which is reviewed and then defended in a final exam.

If you got your PhD in Italy, you can ask for a permit of 9 to 12 months to look for work or start a business (art. 39-bis.1 of the Immigration Act). You apply when your study permit expires. Conditions include a minimum income, health insurance and registering at the employment office. You can later convert it into a work permit.

h: 11. Places for international students and students at risk
x: PhD at Risk (University of Padova): in the 42nd cycle, 3 scholarships for candidates at risk because of conflict, persecution or human rights violations, including refugees and asylum seekers. The scholarship was €17,443 or €18,643 gross a year, with help to arrive and settle in Italy. The call closed on 5 June 2026. University of Cagliari: some places are reserved for holders of foreign degrees, with the interview online by default. University for Foreigners of Siena: 2 places reserved for holders of a scholarship from a foreign government, with the interview online. University of Florence, Pegaso programmes: international candidates could receive a one-off grant of up to €5,000 from Fondazione CR Firenze. Candidates had to be under 35 with English at about B2 level.

Write to a professor who could supervise you, months before the call, and link your project to the programme's research topics. Read every line of the annex: a missing document means exclusion. Apply to more than one university: the dates are spread over the year.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
x: Scholarships in Italy for refugees, people with international or temporary protection, students from countries in conflict and researchers at risk, and how to have your studies recognised without documents. Important. Most of the calls on this page are closed, but most of them come back every year. Use the dates below to know when to look, and always read the current call on the university's site. Many of these scholarships are only for students who are already in Italy or already enrolled: check the residence conditions in each call. For scholarships for Palestinian students, see our guide on Palestinian students.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
h: 1. If you are a refugee or have protection in Italy
x: These scholarships are for people with international protection (refugee status or subsidiary protection) and, in some cases, temporary protection. MUR-CRUI scholarships (Ministry of University and Research and the Conference of Italian University Rectors): 100 scholarships in 2025/26 for students with international protection enrolled at an Italian university. The 2025/26 call closed on 10 August 2025. You applied with an online form and sent the documents to refugees@crui.it. Scholarships for art and music students (AFAM): the Ministry funded 300 scholarships of about €7,000 each for students with international or temporary protection at AFAM institutions, with up to 15% more for an ISEE up to €13,974.30. You apply through your academy or conservatory, which publishes its own call. University of Brescia, 2026/27: 13 scholarships: €4,800 a year, no university fees, discounted meals and transport, and a few places in university housing. There are also places for the Foundation Year. You must already have protection in Italy, even temporary, when you apply. The call closed on 30 September 2026. University of Turin, UniTo for Students at Risk: 10 scholarships of €11,000 (2025/26) for refugees enrolling for the first time, with international, temporary or special protection.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
h: If you lost the documents for your studies
x: The European Qualifications Passport for Refugees (EQPR) assesses your studies through a questionnaire and an interview, with CIMEA, the Italian centre for the recognition of qualifications. It is valid for 5 years. You do not apply on your own: the participating universities choose the candidates, so ask your university's international office.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
h: 2. If you are a refugee outside Italy: UNICORE
x: UNICORE (University Corridors for Refugees) brings refugees to Italian universities for a master's degree, with UNHCR. UNICORE 8.0 (2026/27): 78 scholarships at 41 universities, for refugees living in 13 countries in Africa and South Asia (for example Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda and India). It covers travel, accommodation and university fees. Applications were open from 2 March to 17 April 2026, on universitycorridors.unhcr.it. Watch the portal for the next call and its list of countries. See also our guide on volunteering and other ways to come to Italy.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
h: 3. If you come from a country in conflict
x: You do not always need refugee status for these scholarships. University For What it offered Closed on Politecnico di Torino Students already enrolled there from countries in conflict, including Iran, Afghanistan, Ukraine, Palestine, Sudan, Syria and Yemen 150 scholarships of €1,000, based on credits and grades 15 May 2026 University of Turin Students from countries affected by armed conflict in the last 12 months, with financial difficulties No university fees, and a scholarship of up to €2,000 2025/26 University of Florence Students who live in countries affected by armed conflict €15,000 for each year of the course (in the 2024 edition, winners came from Somalia, Ukraine, Afghanistan and Palestine) December 2024 University of Palermo (Just Peace) Students from countries at war or in a severe internal crisis 20 scholarships of €2,000 10 April 2026 University of Siena (Just Peace) People seeking protection or coming from crisis areas A scholarship, no fees, meals and a laptop No call open now

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
x: University of Padova, PhD at Risk: PhD scholarships for candidates at risk, including refugees and asylum seekers (closed 5 June 2026). See our PhD guide. Scholars at Risk Italy: universities in this network (for example Trento, Verona, Trieste, Pisa and Brescia) offer research fellowships to academics at risk. Sapienza University of Rome, Solidarity in Research and Education: visiting grants of €9,000 for 90 days for scholars from priority countries of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

t: Scholarships for refugees and students from conflict areas
x: The Italian Government scholarships (MAECI) have no special conditions for refugees or conflict areas. The only reserved scheme is the Attanasio scheme, for applicants from Morocco, Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Universities also have their own funds for students in difficulty. Ask the international office or the right-to-study office of your university. See also scholarships and funding and the scholarships directory.

How to apply for your student residence permit after you arrive, how to renew it, and what comes after graduation. Your study visa lets you enter Italy. To stay, you need a residence permit for study (permesso di soggiorno per studio). The steps below are the general rules; your university's international office can help you with the local details.
You must apply within 8 working days of arriving in Italy, to the Questura (police headquarters) of the city where you live. You start the application at the post office.

Get the yellow kit (kit giallo) at a post office with a "Sportello Amico" desk. The form inside (modulo 1) is in Italian only. Fill it in with black ink and block capitals. Patronati and CAF offices often help for free, and many universities have a help desk. Prepare copies of your passport data pages, your visa and your entry stamp, a €16 revenue stamp (marca da bollo, sold at tobacconists), a copy of your health insurance and, if your Questura asks for them, proof of accommodation and of money. Take the kit to the post office with your passport and send it from there. What it costs. For example, the University of Pisa lists for a one-year permit: the €16 revenue stamp, €30 paid at the post office when you send the kit, and a payment slip of €70.46. Check the current amounts at the post office. Keep your receipt. It shows the date of your Questura appointment and your login for the Polizia di Stato website, where you can follow your application. Together with your passport, it proves that you are in Italy legally while you wait.

At the appointment the police take your fingerprints and check your documents. Bring your passport, the post office receipt, the originals of your documents and passport photos (Pisa asks for 2). Some Questure accept only an official enrolment certificate, not a self-declaration.

You will get a message, or see on the website, when the permit is ready. Bring your passport and the original post office receipt. Waiting times depend on the city: Sapienza mentions about 90 days, and Pisa about 3 to 4 months.

Apply at least 90 days before your permit expires (the legal deadline since 22 May 2026; some older documents still say 60 days), again through the post office. You need proof of enrolment and of exams passed: at least one exam in your first year and at least two in later years. One exam may be enough for serious, documented health reasons or force majeure. You can renew for at most three years beyond the normal length of your programme. If your new permit is not ready when the old one expires, your renewal receipt lets you stay legally.

With a study permit you may work up to 20 hours per week, up to 1,040 hours per year. To travel to other Schengen countries you need a valid permit, not just a receipt. With only a receipt, you can usually travel to your home country and back on direct flights only (no stop in another Schengen country), and only if you also have your valid multi-entry visa (first permit) or your expired permit (renewal). Ask your university's international office or the border police before you travel.

If you graduate in Italy (bachelor's, master's, PhD and some other diplomas), you can ask for a permit to look for work or start a business when your study permit expires. It lasts 9 to 12 months. You need enough income and health insurance, and you must declare that you are available for work at the employment services (Centro per l'Impiego). If you find a job, you can ask to convert it into a work permit, if you meet the conditions. See also the study visa guide.

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
x: First time thinking about studying in Italy and not sure where to begin? Read this page first. Simple steps, in order, with no difficult words. This page is for you if you have never applied to a university abroad and you don't know where to start. Go through it slowly, one step at a time. You don't need to understand everything today. The other guides on this site give the full details. Here we only explain what each step means and what to do now.

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Before you start: three things to know
x: Start early. Some deadlines, such as university applications and scholarships, close months before classes begin. Always trust the official page. Rules and dates can change every year. The university's website, Universitaly and the Italian embassy are the sources that count. Our guides link to them. The official portal is free. Pre-enrolment on Universitaly costs nothing. Be careful with anyone who asks you for money to do it for you.

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
x: Bachelor's degree (laurea triennale): the first university degree, after secondary school. Master's degree (laurea magistrale): the degree after a bachelor's. Universitaly: the official Italian website where non-EU students fill in their pre-enrolment. CIMEA statement or Declaration of Value (Dichiarazione di valore): a document that shows what your diploma or degree is worth in Italy. DSU: the regional scholarship. It can give you money, and sometimes a room and meals. Study visa (type D): the visa you need to enter Italy to study. Residence permit (permesso di soggiorno): the document that lets you stay in Italy after you arrive. Codice fiscale: your Italian tax code. You need it for many things, like buying a SIM card.

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 1: Decide what you want to study, and in which language
x: Ask yourself two questions: What level? A bachelor's (after secondary school) or a master's (after a bachelor's)? What subject? Write down two or three subjects you like. Then think about the language. Many programs are taught in English, others in Italian. Both usually ask for at least level B2 in that language. Do now: write on a sheet of paper: the level, two or three subjects, and the language you can study in. If your English is not strong yet, EngPro offers free English lessons with volunteer teachers. Read more: Language requirements

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
x: There are three easy places to look: Universitaly (universitaly.it): its official search covers all the programs in Italy. Our university guide and the map of cities: each university page links to its official list of programs. The university's own website. Once you find a program you like, open its page on the university site. How to search on Google (tips): Write in English, for example: master's degree in economics taught in English Italy. Add the name of the university and international students admission, for example: University of Bologna international students admission. Open the university's own website, not a random blog or video. Information on unofficial pages is often old. Do now: make a simple table with these columns: program name, university, city, language, deadline, link. Add every program you like. Three to five programs is a good start.

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 3: Check that you meet the requirements
x: On each program page, look for the section called admission requirements (or requisiti di accesso in Italian). Usually: For a bachelor's: a secondary school certificate after at least 12 years of school. For a master's: a bachelor's degree, and your transcript (the list of your exams and grades). A language certificate, often at B2 level. Some programs have an entrance exam or special admission rules, for example Architecture or Medicine. Do now: for each program in your table, write yes or no: do I meet the requirements? Read more: How to apply and Admission tests

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
x: Start this early, because some documents take time. Usually you need: Your passport. Your diploma or degree, and for a master's your transcript. A CIMEA statement or a Declaration of Value from the Italian embassy. Translations where needed. Your language certificate. Do now: make a folder on your phone or computer and scan every document into it. Give each file a clear name. Read more: How to apply, section 2

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 5: Think about money and scholarships
x: Studying in Italy has costs: university fees, rent, food. For the visa you must also show that you have enough money. The good news: there are scholarships. The biggest one for most students is the regional DSU scholarship. It depends on your family's income. Its deadlines are often before classes start, so check them as soon as you choose your university. Do now: open the scholarship finder on the funding page, answer the questions and see which scholarships may fit you. Read more: Scholarships and funding and How much it costs

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 6: Apply to the university, then on Universitaly
x: This happens in two parts: Apply to the university, usually through its own online portal, before its deadline. The university checks your documents and decides. Fill in your pre-enrolment on Universitaly. The university then validates it online. Without a validated pre-enrolment, you cannot apply for a study visa. Do now: write the application deadline of each university in your table, and put a reminder in your phone's calendar. Read more: How to apply, sections 3 and 4

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 7: Apply for your study visa
x: With your validated pre-enrolment, you apply at the Italian embassy or consulate in the country where you live. You need a type D study visa. Book your appointment early. Read more: Study visa

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
h: Step 8: When you arrive in Italy
x: Welcome! In the first days you have a few important tasks: Apply for your residence permit within 8 working days of arriving. Finish your enrolment at the university. Get your codice fiscale, a phone number and a place to live. Read more: Your first weeks in Italy and Residence permit

t: Start here: a guide for complete beginners
x: That is normal, and you are not alone. Use the search box at the top of the site to find a word or a topic. Watch our videos, in Arabic. Send us a message on Instagram and tell us which step you are stuck on.

Who needs a type D study visa, when and where to apply, and which documents to bring. This guide is for students who are not EU citizens and who live outside Italy. It follows the official rules of the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR) for 2026/2027 and 2027/2028. Each embassy publishes its own checklist, so always follow the list of the embassy or consulate where you apply.

You need a type D (long-stay) study visa for university enrolment ("Immatricolazione Università") if you are not an EU citizen and you live outside Italy. You do not need one if you are an EU citizen, or if you already live legally in Italy with a residence permit that lets you enrol (ask your university's international office).
You can apply for the visa only after your pre-enrolment on Universitaly has been validated by your university. See How to apply for those steps.

Where: at the Italian embassy or consulate in the country where you live. Many embassies take appointments through Prenot@mi; some use an external visa centre. Your embassy's website says which. You can check which documents you need, and find your embassy, on the official Visa for Italy website. When: for 2026/2027, by 30 November 2026; for 2027/2028, by 31 October 2027. Your university may set an earlier date. Apply early. Appointments can be hard to get, and you need time to collect documents and translations. Since 11 January 2025, your fingerprints are taken when you apply for a national visa.

The exact list depends on the embassy, but you usually need: Passport valid for at least 3 months after the visa ends, with copies of the data pages. Visa application form (type D), filled in and signed, and a recent passport photo (ICAO format). Your Universitaly pre-enrolment summary, validated by the university. Your school diploma (or degree, for a master's), with a CIMEA statement or a Dichiarazione di valore. Your language certificate: Italian B2 for programmes taught in Italian, or a certificate in the teaching language. See Language requirements. Proof of money: for 2026/2027 the national amount is €10,179.85 per year, from legal and traceable sources, preferably yours or your family's (for example a bank statement, with a sponsor letter if the account is a parent's). Proof of accommodation in Italy, such as a rental contract, a hotel booking for the first weeks, or a confirmed place in a student residence. An application for a residence alone is not enough. Health insurance for your stay. A flight booking to Italy. The receipt for the visa fee. Two embassies that publish it list €50; check the amount at yours. Some embassies ask for two copies of every document. Read your embassy's list carefully before the appointment.

The visa is usually valid for 365 days with multiple entries. If you must come to Italy for an in-person entrance exam or language test, you first get a visa valid for 100 days. Within 8 working days of arriving in Italy, apply for your residence permit. See the residence permit guide. Complete your enrolment at the university. If you are not enrolled on Universitaly by 31 January of the academic year, your visa will be revoked and the Questura informed.

A university admission does not guarantee the visa, and the visa does not guarantee enrolment. Keep copies of everything you submit, and keep your Universitaly login. If something on your embassy's list is unclear, write to the embassy before your appointment, not after.

t: Volunteering and other ways to come to Italy
x: The European Solidarity Corps, Italy's civil service, the volunteering visa, university corridors for refugees and humanitarian corridors: who can take part and where to apply. Important. These programmes change their rules, countries and dates every year. We checked everything on this page on the official pages linked below each section, but always read the official page and the current call before you apply. Corso Italy is not linked to any of these programmes. Real volunteering programmes are free: never pay anyone who promises you a "volunteer visa" or a place in a programme.

t: Volunteering and other ways to come to Italy
x: The European Solidarity Corps is the European Union's volunteering programme. Volunteers work full time on a project, for example with young people, migrants, the environment or culture, in another country. Age: you must be at least 18 and not older than 30 when the activity starts. Who can take part: young people who live in the EU and in the countries listed on the programme's countries page. These include the South Mediterranean countries: Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine, Syria and Tunisia. The limit for these countries: volunteers from countries that are not associated with the programme, including the South Mediterranean countries, can join volunteering projects in the EU, but a project may use at most 25% of its grant for them. So most projects in Italy only accept volunteers from EU countries. Each opportunity lists the countries it accepts: check that yours is there. Length: an individual activity is full time (30 to 38 hours a week), and all your activities together can last at most 12 months. Volunteering teams last up to 2 months. What is covered: taking part is free. You get travel to the project and back, free accommodation, food or a food allowance, local transport, pocket money for personal expenses, insurance, training and free online language courses. It is not a salary. Visa: if you need a visa for Italy, ask the host organisation how it will support your application before you accept a place. How to apply Create a profile on the European Solidarity Corps portal. Search for opportunities in Italy and open each one: the page shows which countries it accepts. Contact an accredited organisation in your own country. SALTO EuroMed has information for the South Mediterranean countries. Official pages: portal · countries covered · programme guide 2026

t: Volunteering and other ways to come to Italy
x: A year of volunteering in Italy with associations, municipalities and other organisations, with a monthly allowance. It is not a way to come to Italy: it is open only to people who already live in Italy legally. Who can take part: Italian and EU citizens, and non-EU citizens who live legally in Italy (regolarmente soggiornanti), for example with a residence permit for study. Age: 18 to 28 on the day you apply. Length and allowance: projects last 10 to 12 months, with a monthly allowance of €519.47 (2026 call). How to apply: online only, on the national platform (DOL), with SPID or CIE. Foreign residents without SPID can ask for login details. You can apply for one project only. When: there is usually one big national call a year. The 2026 call closed on 8 April 2026. Official page: information on the 2026 call (Umbria Region)

t: Volunteering and other ways to come to Italy
x: Italian law has a visa for volunteering programmes of social benefit run by Italian non-profit organisations. Age: 25 to 35. Places: limited to a quota set by ministerial decree. Conditions: a written agreement with an Italian non-profit host organisation, which must take out insurance for you (health, accidents and liability) and pay for your travel, food and accommodation. Permit: it lasts as long as the programme, normally up to one year. You cannot apply on your own: the host organisation starts the process. Official text: Legislative Decree 71/2018, art. 27-bis

t: Volunteering and other ways to come to Italy
x: UNICORE brings refugee students to Italian universities for a master's degree, with UNHCR, the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Caritas, Diaconia Valdese and many universities. Who can apply: people recognised as refugees who live in the countries listed in each year's call. In UNICORE 8.0 (2026/27) these were countries in Africa and South Asia. You need a degree that gives access to the master's, obtained in or after 2020, and good grades. Corso Italy is a free, volunteer-run project that helps Arab students study and live in Italy. We collect clear, step-by-step information in Arabic, English and French and link to the official sources. We also run EngPro, a free initiative where volunteer teachers help students improve their English.

In 2025 I went to Lesvos, in Greece, to complete an internship with refugees living in the Mavrovouni camp, as part of my master's degree in Human Rights and Conflict Management in Italy. There I met people from many countries who had risked their lives to cross the sea by boat. They lived through fear. Many had lost loved ones, family members and friends, and had survived against the odds. Part of my work was as a cultural mediator, interpreting between them and the organisations. Doing this, I listened to their stories and their pain. I saw their tears and heard their voices tremble. It affected me deeply. When many of them learned that I came from Syria and was studying in Italy, they told me they had not known that studying was a way to come. Some thought it was almost impossible. Back in Italy to continue my studies, I volunteered as an interpreter with a sea search-and-rescue organisation, and with another organisation in Greece. That is where the idea began: to offer help in a simple, clear way, in three languages, so that people coming from different countries can understand it. This website does more than explain how to come to Italy to study. It also offers free English learning through EngPro. The website is still being developed, and we keep adding to it. — Shahed Hammal, founder of Corso Italy Master in Human Rights and Conflict Management, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna (Pisa)

h: Is Corso Italy free? Is it an agency?

We take our facts mainly from official sources (the Ministry of University and Research, embassies and universities), and each guide shows its sources and the date we last checked it. Rules change often, so always confirm with your university or embassy before you act.

h: Do I need to speak Italian?
x: Not if your programme is taught in English: you usually need English at B2 level instead. For programmes taught in Italian you need Italian at B2 level. See Language requirements.

h: Which English certificate do universities accept?
x: Most ask for B2 level. IELTS Academic, TOEFL iBT, Cambridge English and PTE Academic are the most common. Only some universities accept the Duolingo English Test. See Language requirements.

You choose a programme, apply to the university (often on its own portal), then complete your pre-enrolment on Universitaly. After the university validates it, you apply for the visa. See How to apply.

For a bachelor's degree you need a secondary school diploma obtained after at least 12 years of schooling, with a CIMEA statement or a Dichiarazione di valore and, if your country has a university entrance exam, proof that you passed it. See How to apply.
For 2026/2027, apply for the study visa by 30 November 2026; for 2027/2028, by 31 October 2027. Your university may set an earlier date. See Study visa.

h: How much money do I need to show for the visa?
x: For 2026/2027, €10,179.85 per year, from legal and traceable sources. This is money you must show, not a fee you pay. See How much it costs.

There is no single price. Public universities set fees by family income. For students whose family income is abroad, some universities use a special ISEE and others charge a fixed amount that depends on the country. See How much it costs.
Yes. The main ones are the regional DSU scholarships (based on family income) and the Italian government (MAECI) scholarships. Calls close early. See Scholarships and funding.

h: What do I do when I arrive?
x: Within 8 working days, apply for your residence permit at the post office. Then finish your enrolment and sort out your codice fiscale, health cover and phone. See Your first weeks.

Yes, for the visa and for the residence permit. After you arrive you can keep private insurance or register with the national health service (SSN), which several universities list at €700 per calendar year. See Health insurance.

h: Can I work while I study?
x: Yes, up to 20 hours a week and 1,040 hours a year with a study permit. See Residence permit.

h: How do I find a room and avoid scams?
x: Start with your region's DSU agency and your university's housing office. Never pay before you have seen the room and the contract. See Finding accommodation.

h: Can I stay in Italy after I graduate?
x: If you graduate in Italy, you can ask for a permit to look for work or start a business. It lasts 9 to 12 months, and you need enough income and health insurance. See Residence permit.

Short explanations of the Italian words you will meet when you apply to a university and live in Italy. Italian universities and offices use many Italian words, even on their English pages. Here is what the most common ones mean. Each entry links to the guide that explains it in detail.
The official call for applications of a program or a test. It sets the requirements, the dates and the fees. When a website and the bando disagree, the bando is right.

Accesso libero means open access: there is no limit on places, though there may be a test to check your level. Numero programmato (also called numero chiuso) means limited places, given through a test or a ranking. See admission tests.
Extra learning requirements you receive if your score on an entry test is low. You complete them during your first year, for example with a course or a test.
University credits. One CFU is about 25 hours of study. A full year is usually 60 CFU, and they match the European ECTS credits.
A bachelor's degree, usually three years (180 CFU).
A master's degree, usually two years (120 CFU) after a bachelor's.
A single-cycle degree of five or six years with no separate bachelor's, for example medicine, law or architecture.
The graduatoria is the ranking of candidates after a test or a selection. A scorrimento happens when people give up their places and the next candidates in the ranking are admitted.
An exam session. Most exams have several appelli in a year, and you choose which one to take.
Your final enrolment at the university, after you are admitted and have paid the first instalment.
Pre-enrolment on the Universitaly portal. Non-EU students who live abroad and need a visa must do it before the visa appointment. See how to apply.
A document from the Italian embassy or consulate in the country of your diploma that describes its value in that country's school system.
A statement from CIMEA, the Italian centre for recognising qualifications, that compares your diploma with Italian ones. Many universities accept it instead of the Dichiarazione di valore.
The official stamp that confirms a foreign document is real. Countries that signed the Hague Convention use the apostille; others use legalisation at the Italian consulate.
Your Italian tax code. You need it for almost everything: enrolment, a phone contract, a bank account, a rental contract and health care. See your first weeks.
Italy's digital identity. It lets you log in to public websites (for example INPS or the Agenzia delle Entrate) with one username and password.
The study visa (type D, long stay) that the Italian consulate issues before you travel. See visa.
The residence permit you must request after you arrive in Italy, using the post office kit. See residence permit.
The police headquarters of each province. Its immigration office handles residence permits and takes your fingerprints.

The kit giallo is the yellow envelope with the residence permit form, available at some post offices. When you send it, you get a ricevuta (receipt). Keep it with your passport while you wait for your permit.
A revenue stamp, bought at a tobacconist (tabaccheria), that you stick on some official forms.
The anagrafe is the register of residents at the town hall (comune). Registering your residenza there is separate from the residence permit.
The SSN is Italy's national health service. After you register with it, you get a tessera sanitaria (health card) and can choose a family doctor. See health insurance.
University fees. At public universities, the main part (contributo onnicomprensivo) usually depends on your family's income. See costs.

The ISEE is an indicator of a family's income and assets. Universities and scholarships use it to set fees and decide who gets support. If your family's income is abroad, you usually need an ISEE parificato instead.
An authorised tax help centre. CAF offices prepare the ISEE and the ISEE parificato, often for free or for a small fee.
DSU (diritto allo studio universitario) is the regional right-to-study service. It gives scholarships (borse di studio), housing and meal discounts based on income and merit. See funding.
